title: Type 2 diabetes | NHS inform
text:
Type 2 diabetes
Type 2 diabetes is a common health condition that can cause high blood sugar.
What is blood sugar?
Blood sugar, or glucose, is the main type of sugar in blood. The body uses it for energy. The pancreas, a small body part behind the stomach, makes a hormone called insulin.
Insulin works like a key, letting blood sugar move from blood into the body’s cells to be used for energy.
Why does blood sugar get too high?
With type 2 diabetes, this system doesn’t work as well as it should. This happens in 2 ways. Either the pancreas doesn’t make enough insulin, or the insulin made doesn’t work correctly.
Both of these means sugar stays in the blood instead of going into cells for energy.
Symptoms of type 2 diabetes
People with type 2 diabetes can have no symptoms for a long time. The signs often appear slowly over a few years, so some people don’t realise they have it. It’s often found during a check-up.
Common symptoms include:
feeling very
thirsty
needing to pee more than usual, especially at night
feeling very tired
losing weight without trying
cuts or ulcers that take a long time to heal
blurred vision
repeatedly getting
thrush
If any of these signs appear, it is important to see a healthcare professional as soon as possible.
Causes of type 2 diabetes
Anyone can get type 2 diabetes, but some things make it more likely.
Risk factors that can’t be changed
There are some risk factors that you can’t change that make you more likely to have type 2 diabetes. These include your:
age
family history
family background
It’s more common as people get older.
If a close relative has type 2 diabetes, you’re more likely to develop it.
People from certain family backgrounds are more at risk from a younger age, including:
South Asian
Chinese
African-Caribbean
Black African
Risk factors that can be changed
There are some risk factors that you can change that make you more likely to have type 2 diabetes. These include:
your weight
your lifestyle
Being overweight is a common risk factor, especially if weight is carried around the tummy.
Treating type 2 diabetes
Type 2 diabetes is treated by:
changes to your diet
losing weight
medication
Medication
Some people need medication to treat their type 2 diabetes.
Metformin
Metformin is a common medicine often prescribed first. It helps lower blood sugar towards normal levels, but doesn’t put you at risk of low blood sugars.
Diabetes UK have more information on Metformin
SGLT2 inhibitor (‘flozins)
SGLT2 inhibitor tablets cause your kidneys to release sugar into your pee. This helps lower your blood sugar. These medications are also used for
heart failure
and
kidney disease
.
Diabetes UK have more information on SGLT2 inhibitors
GLP-1 agonists
GLP-1 agonists can be injections or tablets. These help your pancreas make more insulin and can help you make more healthy food choices.
Diabetes UK have move information on GLP-1 agonists
Other medications
There are other medications sometimes used like:
sulphonylureas
such gliclazide
gliptins
pioglitazone
Insulin injections
Some people with type 2 diabetes may need insulin injections. Your diabetes care team will teach you how to inject insulin yourself.
Diabetes UK have more information on insulin
Hypo (hypoglycaemia or low blood glucose)
If you’re using insulin or
sulphonylureas
(like gliclazide), a side affect of these can be something known as a hypo. This is when your blood glucose levels can become too low.
Most people using other medications for type 2 diabetes don’t experience hypos. For this reason you wouldn’t normally be asked to check your blood sugars with a finger prick strip.
Read more about hypoglycaemia
Remission of type 2 diabetes
Remission is when you have a normal, or near normal, blood sugar without using medications.
This is easier to do if you have had type 2 diabetes for less than 10 years.
Your healthcare professional can discuss what options are available to you.
Read more from Diabetes UK about remission
Preventing type 2 diabetes
You are less likely to develop type 2 diabetes if you:
maintain a healthy weight
eat lots of fruit, vegetables, and whole grains
are
more active
don’t smoke
reduce how much alcohol you drink
Living with type 2 diabetes
It’s possible to live a full and healthy life with type 2 diabetes.
You should:
have a care plan that’s been discussed with your healthcare professional
stay active
and
eat well
have blood tests and urine tests every year
have
eye checks
and
feet checks
If remission isn’t possible you might be able to control type 2 diabetes with diet and exercise. Over time many people need medicine. Your healthcare professional will talk to you about your options.
What is the HbA1c test?
The HbA1c is a blood test that your care team will check at least once a year. You may have these more often if you’ve changed medication or developed new symptoms. This test gives your healthcare team an estimate of your blood sugar levels over the last 3 months.
Your healthcare team will help you find a target HbA1c level. If your HbA1c is too high or too low, your treatment plan might need to change.
My Diabetes My Way has a video on
Hba1c tests and reducing your risk of complications
.
Checking your blood sugar at home
You might also be asked to check your blood sugar yourself at home using a small machine called a blood glucose meter.
Checks are important if you take
insulin
or
sulphonylureas
(like gliclazide) that could cause your blood sugar to go too low (known as a hypo).
Your diabetes team will teach you how to use the meter if you need one.
Driving with diabetes
You can drive if you have diabetes, but there are some rules.
Read about driving with diabetes from the DVLA
You must tell your insurance company. This will not stop you from driving, but it is a legal requirement.
If you’re taking a medication that puts you at risk of having a hypo you should be aware of what to do and have a way of checking your blood sugar with you.
If you have a hypo while driving you should:
pull over safely and stop the engine
get out of the driver’s seat
have something sugary to treat the hypo
wait at least 45 minutes after your blood sugar is back to a safe level (5mmol/l or above) before driving again
Diabetes UK have advice and information about driving
Complications of type 2 diabetes
If blood sugar levels stay high for a long time, it can cause other health problems.
These could be:
heart and circulation problems
nerve damage
eye problems
kidney problems
foot problems
sexual problems
You can also help reduce the risk of developing complications by:
having an Hb1Ac at the target level
reducing your
cholesterol
stopping smoking
treating any
high blood pressure
Heart and circulation problems
Over time, high blood sugar can damage the blood vessels. The damage can make them narrow and they can become blocked.
This can lead to heart disease, having a
heart attack
or having a
stroke
.
Nerve damage
High blood sugar can damage the small blood vessels in your nerves.
This can cause a tingling or burning pain, or numbness, most often in your hands and feet.
If you have numbness, it’s important to be extra careful with your feet. Cuts and sores might not be noticed, which can lead to serious infections.
Read more about diabetic foot issues
Eye problems
High blood sugar can damage the tiny blood vessels in the retina, which is the part of the eye that lets you see. This condition is called
diabetic retinopathy
.
To check for this, everyone with diabetes who is over 12 will be invited to
an eye screening
. The screening isn’t painful and takes a picture of the back of your eye. If found early, treatment can help protect your sight.
There are other conditions that can affect your eyes like cataracts.
Don’t wait for your eye screening. If you have any problems or concerns about your eye health you should contact
your optician
.
My Diabetes My Way has
more information about diabetes and eyes
.
Kidney problems
High blood sugar can also harm the tiny blood vessels in your kidneys. This means they don’t work as well.
Regular urine tests and monitoring your
blood pressure
helps to pick up any problems before they become serious.
Read more about kidney disease
Foot problems
Because of poor circulation and nerve damage, cuts or blisters on your feet can get infected more easily. This can lead to problems like foot ulcers.
My Diabetes My Way has information about
how diabetes can affect your feet
.
Your feet will be checked at least every 2 years by your care team. It’s still very important to check your feet every day and tell your doctor or nurse about any changes in-between checks.
Read more about how to look after your feet when you have type 2 diabetes
Sexual problems
Nerve and blood vessel damage can cause:
problems with erections
vaginal dryness
pain during sex
Thrush is more common in people with diabetes.
These issues can often be treated. Speak to your healthcare professional if you’re worried.
Pregnancy with type 2 diabetes
If you have diabetes and are thinking about having a baby, you should talk to your healthcare professional first.
You need to control your blood sugar very well before and during early pregnancy.
Some diabetes tablets are not safe during pregnancy. You may need to switch to insulin injections.
You may need to take a higher dose of folic acid, which helps prevent problems with your baby’s spine. This is only available on prescription.
Pregnancy can put extra pressure on the small blood vessels in your eyes, so it is important to treat any eye problems before you get pregnant.
Support for people with type 2 diabetes
It can help to talk to others who understand what you’re going through.
The charity
Diabetes UK
has local support groups and a helpline.
You can phone Diabetes UK Helpline (Scotland) on 0141 212 8710 Monday to Friday, 9am to 6pm.
Getting financial help
Some people with diabetes may be able to get financial help or benefits. This depends on how diabetes affects your daily life.
Social Security Scotland
can help with applications for benefits. You can phone 0800 182 2222 or talk to their
Webchat
Monday to Friday, 8am to 5pm.
Citizens Advice Scotland
can help check what benefits you might be entitled to. You can phone 0800 028 1456.
Telecare Self-Check online tool
Telecare is the use of equipment that can get you help quickly if you need it.
It can help give you, your family and carers peace of mind. It also can allow you to live more independently in your own home and when you’re outside.
Visit the
Telecare Self-Check online tool
to find the right support for you in your area. This easy to use online tool allows you to find helpful information on telecare services that could help you live independently at home for longer.
